title: Minimum Swaps to Sort

concept.title: Cycles of the permutation
body: Sort the array in your head and note, for each sorted position `k`, the index `order[k]` where the element that belongs there currently sits. This is a **permutation** of the indexes, and it breaks into cycles: a cycle of length `c` means `c` elements that must rotate among `c` places.

One swap can fix at most one cycle step, and a cycle of length `c` needs exactly `c - 1` swaps. Fixed points (cycles of length 1) cost nothing. So the minimum number of swaps is `n` minus the number of cycles.

statement: Given an array of `n` different integers, find the smallest number of swaps (exchanging any two elements, not only neighbours) needed to sort the array in increasing order.
inputFormat: The second line has `n` different integers.
outputFormat: Print the minimum number of swaps.

examples.note: Swap 4 with 1 and 3 with 2: two swaps.

hints: Find where each element must go in the sorted array.
The "should go there" relation splits the positions into cycles.
A cycle of length c needs c - 1 swaps; add them up.

explanation: The positions form cycles under the "belongs there" map. Each cycle of length `c` can be fixed with `c - 1` swaps and not fewer, so the answer is the sum of `c - 1`, i.e. `n` minus the number of cycles.
solution.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: a[i])
visited = [False] * n
swaps = 0
for i in range(n):
    if not visited[i]:
        length = 0
        j = i
        while not visited[j]:
            visited[j] = True
            j = order[j]
            length += 1
        swaps += length - 1
print(swaps)
